title: Ramana Maharshi (Who Am I?)
hook: a visitor asks a silent teacher the oldest question, and the answers come back in writing

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Raja Yoga with Vivekananda's lake: still the waves, and the bottom shows. Did the water settle for you, even for a breath? Today, a new teacher. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

Who are you? Asked at a party, the answer comes easily: a name, a job, a town, somebody's daughter. Asked at three in the morning, it gets harder. In south India, at the foot of a holy hill called Arunachala, a visitor once put that question, and others, to a young teacher who, tradition says, hardly spoke in those years. So the answers came back written down. The little text that grew out of that exchange is called Who Am I?, and the teacher is known as Ramana Maharshi.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU?` → `A VISITOR AT ARUNACHALA.` → `ANSWERS WRITTEN, NOT SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: The text doesn't start with the question. It starts with something everyone can check. Every living being wants to be happy and not to suffer, it says, and everyone loves themselves above all. Happiness, Ramana says, is our real nature, and to find it we need to know ourselves. And the way to know yourself is to ask: who am I? Then comes the answer, and it moves by taking things away. The body is not I, he says. The senses that see and hear and touch are not I. The organs that move and speak are not I. The breath, the life-force moving through you, is not I. Even the mind, the thing that thinks, is not I. Each one gets set down, like taking off layers on a warm day. And then the question: if I am none of these, what am I? What's left, the text says, after all of that is set aside, is awareness, and that, Ramana says, is what I am. It sounds like a riddle, but it works more like a mirror. When you say my hand, my thoughts, my mood, there's someone doing the owning. Ramana's question is aimed at that owner. He doesn't ask you to believe an answer. He asks you to look. The text itself names the old road it's walking: each thing is set aside as not this, not this, the phrase the Upanishads use. Ramana puts it in a few plain pages. Tomorrow, how he says to ask it when the thoughts won't stop.
screen: `EVERYONE WANTS TO BE HAPPY.` · `NOT THE BODY, NOT THE SENSES, NOT THE MIND.` · `WHAT REMAINS IS AWARENESS.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Notice the body, its weight on the seat, and say to yourself quietly: this is noticed. Notice a sound in the room: this is noticed too. Notice a thought passing: also noticed. Now turn, gently, toward whatever is doing the noticing, and ask once, without hurry: who am I? Don't reach for an answer in words. Just rest your attention there, the way you'd rest your eyes on a far horizon. If you pray, you can let that resting be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher of Arunachala whose short text Who Am I? sets down body, senses and mind, and asks what's left.
Your line: Ramana Maharshi, Who Am I? Today, the next time you say my, my phone, my plans, my bad mood, pause and ask quietly who's doing the owning. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: People who follow Ramana's teaching practice self-inquiry, turning attention back to the sense of 'I' and asking 'who am I?'; Who Am I? is read and recited at his ashram at the foot of Arunachala in Tiruvannamalai and by readers around the world.

fork.reveal: in Who Am I?, after everything is set aside, awareness alone remains, and Ramana says that is the I.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: vichara, inquiry. Ramana's way is often called atma-vichara, inquiry into the self.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'who am I?' is a question about your personality.
what it means: Ramana sets down body, senses, breath and mind as 'not I', and points to the awareness that remains.
what a scholar hears: the text grew from a visitor's questions, answered in writing at Arunachala, and it walks an old Upanishadic road in plain words.

sources.ref: Who Am I? (Nan Yar), the opening and the first answer (body, senses, breath and mind set aside as 'not I'; awareness remains)

notes: All paraphrase; English translations of Nan Yar (e.g. T. M. P. Mahadevan's) are under copyright. Confirm the opening (all beings desire happiness; love for oneself; happiness is one's nature; inquiry 'who am I?' as the means) and the negation list.

The setting (questions from a visitor, traditionally named as Sivaprakasam Pillai, answered in writing because Ramana was largely silent then) is attributed to tradition; the visitor is unnamed in the script on purpose.

Editor pass: replaced the claim about what the listener met in an earlier year, and the narrator's praise ('Ramana's gift was...'), with the text's own 'not this, not this' (neti neti) wording. Confirm Nan Yar uses 'neti neti' in the negation passage and that it is fair to call it the Upanishads' phrase (Brihadaranyaka).
Original-game word 'vichara' / 'atma-vichara' as a name for Ramana's method: confirm.
